q: The SI unit of angular acceleration is:
x: Angular acceleration = change in angular velocity (rad s⁻¹) ÷ time (s), so its unit is rad s⁻². rad s⁻¹ is the unit of angular velocity, the usual mix-up.

q: A point on a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω is at a distance r from the axis. Its linear (tangential) speed v is given by:
x: Arc length s = rθ; dividing by time gives v = rω. rω² is the centripetal acceleration, not the speed.

q: A ceiling fan turns at a steady 300 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is:
x: 300 rev min⁻¹ = 5 rev s⁻¹, and each revolution is 2π rad, so ω = 5 × 2π = 10π rad s⁻¹. Forgetting to divide by 60 gives 600π rad s⁻¹; taking one revolution as π rad gives 5π.

q: A wheel of radius 25 cm rotates so that a point on its rim moves at 5 m s⁻¹. The angular velocity of the wheel is:
x: ω = v/r = 5/0.25 = 20 rad s⁻¹ (check: 0.25 × 20 = 5 m s⁻¹). Leaving the radius in centimetres gives 5/25 = 0.2 rad s⁻¹; multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.25.

q: A flywheel speeds up uniformly from 20 rad s⁻¹ to 50 rad s⁻¹ in 10 s. The angle it turns through in this time is:
x: For uniform angular acceleration θ = ½(ωi + ωf)t = ½(20 + 50) × 10 = 350 rad (check: α = 3 rad s⁻², θ = 20 × 10 + ½ × 3 × 100 = 350 rad). Using only the final angular velocity gives 500 rad.

q: The minute hand and the hour hand of a clock both turn steadily. The ratio of the angular velocity of the minute hand to that of the hour hand is:
x: The minute hand makes one revolution in 1 h and the hour hand in 12 h. Since ω = 2π/T, the ratio is 12 : 1. Putting the periods the wrong way round gives 1 : 12.

q: A wheel turning at 12 rad s⁻¹ is slowed by a uniform angular retardation of 3 rad s⁻² until it stops. The angle it turns through while stopping is:
x: ωf² = ωi² − 2αθ gives 0 = 144 − 6θ, so θ = 24 rad (check: it stops in 4 s at an average of 6 rad s⁻¹, 6 × 4 = 24 rad). Dropping the factor 2 gives 48 rad; 4 is the stopping time in seconds.

q: A wheel starts from rest and turns with uniform angular acceleration. In the first 10 s it turns through 100 rad. Through what angle does it turn in the next 10 s?
x: From rest θ = ½αt², so θ ∝ t²: in 20 s it turns 4 × 100 = 400 rad, so in the second 10 s it turns 400 − 100 = 300 rad (check: α = 2 rad s⁻²). 400 rad is the total for 20 s; 100 rad assumes constant angular velocity.

q: A disc of radius 0.2 m has an angular acceleration of 15 rad s⁻². The tangential acceleration of a point on its rim is:
x: a_t = rα = 0.2 × 15 = 3 m s⁻². Dividing α by r instead of multiplying gives 75 m s⁻².

q: A wheel spinning about a fixed axis is slowing down. The direction of its angular acceleration is:
o: Along the axis, opposite to the angular velocity
Along the axis, in the same direction as the angular velocity
Along the tangent to the rim, opposite to the motion of the rim
Along the radius, towards the centre of the wheel
x: Angular velocity and angular acceleration are axial vectors along the axis of rotation. When the wheel slows down, the change in ω points opposite to ω, so α is along the axis opposite to ω. The tangent and radius describe linear accelerations of rim points, not α.

q: A car moves at 15 m s⁻¹ on wheels of radius 0.25 m that roll without slipping. Taking π ≈ 3.14, each wheel turns at about:
x: ω = v/r = 15/0.25 = 60 rad s⁻¹ = 60/(2 × 3.14) ≈ 9.55 rev s⁻¹ ≈ 573 rev min⁻¹. Dividing by π instead of 2π gives 1146; 60 is the value in rad s⁻¹, not rev min⁻¹.

q: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, how are its angular velocity and the linear velocity of a point on the body (not on the axis) related in direction?
o: They are parallel to each other
They are perpendicular to each other
They are inclined at 45° to each other
x: Angular velocity points along the axis (right-hand rule), while the linear velocity of a point is tangent to its circle, which lies in a plane perpendicular to the axis. So they are perpendicular (v = ω × r).

q: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of:
x: Angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt, the rate of change of angular velocity. The rate of change of angular displacement is the angular velocity itself.

q: A turntable starts from rest with a uniform angular acceleration of 4π rad s⁻². How many revolutions does it make in the first 5 s?
x: θ = ½αt² = ½ × 4π × 25 = 50π rad, and one revolution is 2π rad, so it makes 50π/2π = 25 revolutions. Forgetting the ½ gives 50.

q: A wheel of radius 0.4 m starts from rest with an angular acceleration of 5 rad s⁻². How far does a point on its rim travel along its circular path in the first 4 s?
x: θ = ½αt² = ½ × 5 × 16 = 40 rad, so the arc length s = rθ = 0.4 × 40 = 16 m. Giving the angle 40 as metres, or forgetting the ½ (32 m), are the usual slips; 8 is the rim speed in m s⁻¹ at 4 s.

q: A body moves in a circle at constant speed. Its centripetal acceleration is:
o: Constant in both magnitude and direction
Zero, because the speed is constant
Constant in magnitude but changing in direction
Changing in magnitude but fixed in direction
x: a = v²/r has a fixed size, but it always points to the centre, so its direction keeps turning with the body. Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration, because the velocity's direction changes.

q: A body moves at constant speed in a circle. The centripetal force on it does no work because:
o: It is balanced by an equal outward force
It is always parallel to the body's velocity
The body's kinetic energy is zero
It is always perpendicular to the body's velocity
x: Work = Fd cos θ, and the centripetal force always acts along the radius, at 90° to the velocity, so cos 90° = 0 and no work is done; the speed and kinetic energy stay constant. A force parallel to the velocity would change the speed.

q: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.8 m on a smooth table, held by a string that breaks if the tension exceeds 40 N. The greatest speed the stone can have is:
x: The tension supplies the centripetal force: T = mv²/r, so v² = Tr/m = 40 × 0.8/0.5 = 64 and v = 8 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 64 m s⁻¹.

q: A car of mass 1000 kg crosses the top of a hump-backed bridge, curved as a vertical circle of radius 20 m, at 10 m s⁻¹. The upward force of the road on the car at the top is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: At the top the net downward force is the centripetal force: mg − N = mv²/r, so N = 10000 − 1000 × 100/20 = 10000 − 5000 = 5000 N. Adding mv²/r, as at the bottom of a dip, gives 15000 N; ignoring the circular motion gives 10000 N.

q: A wheel of radius 0.5 m turns at 600 rev min⁻¹. The centripetal acceleration of a point on its rim is:
x: 600 rev min⁻¹ = 10 rev s⁻¹, so ω = 20π rad s⁻¹ and a = rω² = 0.5 × 400π² = 200π² m s⁻² (about 2000 m s⁻²). Forgetting to square ω gives 10π; using 10 rev s⁻¹ as ω gives 50 m s⁻²; leaving out r gives 400π².

q: The SI unit of angular momentum is:
x: L = Iω, with I in kg m² and ω in s⁻¹ (radian is dimensionless), so L is in kg m² s⁻¹ (= J s). kg m s⁻¹ is linear momentum and kg m² is moment of inertia.

q: A 0.2 kg ball tied to a string moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m at a speed of 3 m s⁻¹. Its angular momentum about the centre is:
x: L = mvr = 0.2 × 3 × 0.5 = 0.3 kg m² s⁻¹ (check: I = mr² = 0.05 kg m², ω = v/r = 6 rad s⁻¹, Iω = 0.3). Dividing by r instead of multiplying gives 1.2.

q: Two small 1 kg masses are fixed at the ends of a light rod 2 m long. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis through the middle of the rod, perpendicular to it, is:
x: Each mass is 1 m from the axis: I = Σmr² = 1 × 1² + 1 × 1² = 2 kg m². Using the full 2 m length for each mass gives 8 kg m²; 4 kg m² is the value about an axis through one of the masses.

q: A uniform disc spins freely on a smooth vertical axle. An identical disc, not spinning, is dropped gently onto it on the same axle, and the two then turn together. What fraction of the original rotational kinetic energy is lost?
x: Angular momentum is conserved: Iω = 2Iω′, so ω′ = ω/2. New KE = ½(2I)(ω/2)² = ¼Iω², half of the original ½Iω², so one half is lost (to friction between the discs). Answering zero confuses conservation of angular momentum with conservation of kinetic energy.

q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 2 kg m² has an angular momentum of 8 kg m² s⁻¹. Its rotational kinetic energy is:
x: ω = L/I = 4 rad s⁻¹, so KE = ½Iω² = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J (check: KE = L²/2I = 64/4 = 16 J). Forgetting the ½ gives 32 J; 4 is ω, not the energy.

q: The orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit round the Earth does NOT depend on the:
x: Setting GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r): the satellite's mass m cancels, while the Earth's mass M, the orbit radius r and G all appear.

q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 1.6 × 10⁷ m round a planet, where the planet's gravitational field strength is 4 N kg⁻¹. Its orbital speed is:
x: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: mg′ = mv²/r, so v = √(g′r) = √(4 × 1.6 × 10⁷) = √(64 × 10⁶) = 8 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 6.4 × 10⁷; √(r/g′) gives 2 × 10³.

q: A geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the Earth's surface. Its orbit must be:
o: In the equatorial plane, moving from east to west
A polar orbit, passing over both poles
In the equatorial plane, moving from west to east
In any plane through the Earth's centre, moving from west to east
x: To stay over one point it must turn with the Earth: the same 24 h period, the same sense of rotation (west to east) and an orbit in the equatorial plane. An orbit in any other plane would carry it north and south of the equator during each day.

q: Satellite P orbits a planet in a circular orbit of radius r with period T. Satellite Q orbits the same planet in a circular orbit of radius 9r. The period of Q is:
x: v = √(GM/r), so T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM) and T ∝ r^(3/2): 9^(3/2) = 27, so Q's period is 27T (check: Q's speed is v/3 over a path 9 times as long, 9 × 3 = 27). Using T ∝ √r gives 3T; T ∝ r gives 9T.

q: A satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface has a speed of 8 km s⁻¹. Another satellite orbits at a height above the surface equal to the Earth's radius. Its orbital speed is:
x: The second orbit has radius R + R = 2R, and v = √(GM/r) ∝ 1/√r, so v = 8/√2 = 4√2 ≈ 5.7 km s⁻¹. Taking v ∝ 1/r gives 4 km s⁻¹; forgetting that a higher orbit is slower gives 8√2.
